units.translation: Hesychius ῥύσια [things seized as surety, means of deliverance, ransoms, plunderings]: ἐνεχυράσματα [pledges], σωτήρια [means of safety], λύτρα [ransoms], λεηλασίαι [plunderings]. Similarly other grammarians: see Etym. M. p. 706, 40, Photius, Suidas, Zonaras p. 1622, the scholiast on Homer Il. 11, 673, Eustathius p. 877, 35 and on Dionysius Periegetes 527. On their explanations Hermann in his note on Ag. 513 (535) vol. 2 p. 410: "These matters have not been explained sufficiently clearly by the grammarians. ῥύσιον [a thing seized as surety], formed from ῥύεσθαι [to protect, deliver], properly means a thing taken away, which must be claimed by force and thus kept safe. So Aeschylus Suppl. 412 (about the Danaids whom the sons of Aegyptus claim for themselves) καὶ μήτε δῆρις ῥυσίων ἐφάψεται — [and let no strife lay hold of the sureties] —. 728 ἄγειν θέλοντες ῥυσίων ἐφάπτορες [wishing to lead them away, laying hold of the sureties]. (where the scholium has ἐνεχύρων [of pledges]. ἐνεχυράζοντες ἡμᾶς διά τινος ἁρπαγῆς [taking us as pledges through some seizure].) So in Sophocles Oed. Col. 858. Creon, dragging Oedipus away together with his daughters, says, καὶ μεῖΖον ἀρα ῥύσιον πόλει τάχα θήσεις ? ἐφάψομαι γὰρ οὐ ταύταιν μόναιν [will you then soon make a greater seizure for the city? For I will lay hold not of these two alone]. In this way also in Ag. 535 Helen, having been seized by Paris and claimed by the Greeks, is called ῥύστον [a thing seized as surety], τοῦ ῥυσίου θ᾽ ἥμαρτε [and he missed the surety]. The second meaning is that of a pledge, which is taken in place of the thing that has been taken away. So in Il. 11, 673 ῥύσι᾿ ἐλαυνόμενος [driving off cattle as surety]. From this arises a third meaning, which is that of satisfaction or vengeance, when a pledge, if the thing itself cannot be restored, is used to give satisfaction to the injured party. So Sophocles in Phil. 959 φόνον φόνου δὲ ῥύσιον τίσω τάλας [I, wretched, will pay murder as a surety for murder]. There is a fourth meaning, derived from the first, by which the liberation of a thing from another's power and its restoration to its original state is indicated. So Io, when she had become pregnant with Epaphus by the touch of Zeus and had recovered her human form, Aeschylus called that restoration of form ῥύσια [means of deliverance] in Suppl. 314. Ἔπαφος ἀληθῶς ῥυσίων ἐπώνυμος [Epaphus truly named from the deliverance]. From this finally comes a fifth use, by which whatever is done for safety is understood, and in this way the word is to be taken in Dionysius Periegetes 527 ῥύσια δ᾽ Ἀπόλλωνι χοροὺς ἀνάγουσιν ἅπασαι [and all the women lead up choirs as thank-offerings to Apollo]."
